newsitem.title: UK: Post Kleinwort, Mercury carries privatisation torch. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Post Kleinwort, Mercury carries privatisation torch. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: As the 500 million pound Kleinwort European Privatisation Investment Trust Plc heads for an early grave, many commentators have denounced European privatisation funds as a worthless concept.

"You might as well select all shares beginning with the letter "B'," quipped Stephen Peak, who manages the TR European Growth Trust which put the final nail in the Kleinwort Trust's coffin when it launched a hostile takeover bid for the trust.

Yet, for the Mercury European Privatisation Trust which has assets of 693 million pounds ($1.08 billion) and was launched at approximately the same time as the Kleinwort trust, these charges are untrue and hurtful.

"Investing in privatisations is the same as investing in other stocks. You do your research and buy good companies. You don't plunge into stocks like Renault and French banks," said Paul Harwood who manages the Mercury fund.

It is stocks such as Renault which have given European privatisation a bad name, the French carmaker's shares have slumped from their 165 French franc ($31.93) a share offer price in 1994 to just 110 francs now.
For the 77,000 small investors in the KEPIT fund, European privatisations may have been a step too far, said Fiona Price, managing director of independent financial advisor Fiona Price Associates.
"There was a very big marketing campaign based on the huge gains generated by the success of the British privatision programme of the 1980s," she said.
Mercury's Harwood points to a steady, if unexciting performance from his fund.

The net asset value of the Mercury fund is up 37.5 percent on a total return basis compared with a 14.1 percent rise in the benchmark MSCI Europe Index and despite a share buyback launched earlier this year, the Mercury trust is still alive. (Corrects figures to show net asset value performance instead of share value).

By November this year, the the Kleinwort trust will cease to exist, with investors opting for a cash exit, a new Kleinwort European privatisation unit trust, or a general European trust managed by M&G Plc.

Harwood believes that the action which precipitated the Kleinwort investment trust's collapse may have come just as the corner is turning in Europe and notes that these trusts were founded on a longer investment view than two years.
"People are becoming far too obsessed with short-term performance. In the light of recent events in the fund management industry, steady performance is probably not such a bad thing," said Harwood.
Three European unit trusts managed by Morgan Grenfell Asset Management, part of Germany's Deutche Bank AG, were suspended from trading pending an investigation of "irregularities".
Fiona Price is advising her clients who are invested in the Kleinwort fund to take the cash option or invest in the M&G European fund, whose performance she describes as "steady".
"For people who still want privatisations, there is the Mercury trust, which is on a 14 percent discount to net asset value," she said.
Harwood is looking for a boost to performance from an economic recovery in Europe led by lower exchange rates in France and Germany, which will boost export competitiveness.
Harwood is looking at companies with strong overseas earnings and aims to overweight energy companies within his portfolio at the expense of some existing holdings.

"There is growth in global energy demand, especially from debeloping countries. France's Total has still not been re-rated despite a strong performance, BP is looking good and we may have another look at Enterprise," he said.
He also sees opportunities in the timber and steel sectors.
"One day we may even look at the French banking sector," Harwood says.
